Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash for the respiratory disease specialist drugmaker. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023. In this article INSM SNY IBB XPH PFE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Insmed shares rallied 14% in premarket trading Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023. The acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash. It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff , when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023. Insmed shares rose 14.6% to $170.86 in early premarket trading, while Sanofi stock rose 6% in Paris. 'Buys time' Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside. Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop towards the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete. Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026 , as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets, and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026. While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity. Sanofi/Insmed shares over the past 12 months. "Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday. Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA , Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate , following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results. Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases. "The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition. headlines.article_text: Rene Haas to remain CEO of chipmaker Arm through 2033 amid Nvidia top job chatter Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article USDAUD= ARM NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Rene Haas, chief executive officer of Arm Holdings Plc, speaks during the Arm Everywhere event in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas has extended his contract to lead the chip designer through 2033, confirming his leadership role at the company amid speculation that Nvidia could tap him for the top job after Jensen Huang's resignation. Haas was among several names floated as potential candidates to replace Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's CEO earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia's board had approached Haas in its search for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times had reported. Nvidia's finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO at the company. Analysts also pointed to Haas as a solid candidate for the top job at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company — rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business — before joining Arm in 2013. U.S.-listed shares of Arm were up nearly 9% in premarket trading amid a broader lift in AI stocks as they rebounded after a bruising selloff last week. Haas' standing as a high-profile semiconductor industry figure and his familiarity with Nvidia were seen as key reasons making him a good fit for the CEO role at Nvidia. He became the British chipmaker's CEO in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year. Arm licenses processor designs used across smartphones, PCs, servers and connected devices, and Nvidia relies heavily on the company's chip architecture. "I've never been more confident about Arm's future ... I'm wholly committed to realizing Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday. Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of SoftBank Group, effective December 1, Arm said. Arm is majority-owned by SoftBank. Haas is a board member at the Japanese conglomerate and, in April, took over the reins of SoftBank's international business. headlines.title: Signal joins United Airlines, banks in limiting AI agents over customer risks
headlines.summary: Privacy-focused messaging application Signal has joined United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase in implementing restrictions around artificial intelligence agents.
headlines.article_text: Signal joins United Airlines, banks in limiting AI agents Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Privacy-focused Signal says AI agents built into mobile operating systems can scan information on users' screens, potentially capturing and storing Signal data outside its control. Signal called on Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide simple technical tools and documentation that let developers prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. The move follows restrictions by companies including United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab, which have limited or blocked AI agents over security and customer-protection concerns. Jakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty Images Privacy-focused messaging application Signal is tightening protections against artificial intelligence agents that can access information displayed on users' screens, citing concerns over privacy and security. Signal said AI agents built into mobile operating systems, such as Google's Gemini and Apple's Siri with onscreen awareness, can "scan" information on users' screens, potentially capturing and storing Signal data outside its control. People treat agent risk as one-size-fits-all rather than matching the security needed to the actual task. Yat Siu Co-founder, Animoca Brands The company said it will block screenshots in its iOS app and, on Android, enable screen security when it detects an AI assistant attempting to read the screen. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal — and application developers beyond — lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," Meredith Whittaker, president of the app's nonprofit parent Signal Foundation, said in a Friday blog post . Signal last year introduced similar restrictions against Microsoft's Recall AI on Windows 11. Its latest move adds to a broader push by companies including United Airlines , JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab to limit or block AI agents over security and for customer-protection concerns. Whittaker said the new protections do not address every way an agent might gain access to data, including by retrieving content already stored on a user's device. Signal also warned that third-party agents such as Meta's Muse could gain access to private app content through permissions granted during setup. "Application-level protections will always have gaps, so the data an agent can reach has to be classified, permissioned and recoverable before the agent arrives," said Tianyi Jiang, CEO of data management and protection software company AvePoint. AvePoint's State of AI 2026 report found that 88.4% of surveyed organizations had experienced at least one AI-agent-related security breach in the previous year. The survey covered 750 IT leaders globally. "We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data," said Whittaker. Restricted entry Banks are also restricting third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in October that outside agents were too risky for the bank and its clients. Morgan Stanley has blocked third-party agents from its platforms, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, Charles Schwab CEO Richard Wurster said the brokerage blocks unauthorized agents to protect clients and the firm. Singapore's OCBC Bank has said it will not let third-party agents to interact with the bank to transfer money autonomously and warned that "customers should exercise caution" when using such agents for banking. United Airlines said Nov. 11 that it would restrict unauthorized agents from booking or managing tickets, citing risks that they could expose customer information, make unintended purchases or violate aviation rules. "To book flights or do your grocery shop, an agent needs your email, accounts and payment details," said Mick Maleishko, an AI advocate at identity verification and compliance platform Sumsub. He said that level of access creates a risk of account hijacking because actions taken by an agent may appear to a retailer or bank to have been authorized by the user. Singapore Airlines , by contrast, is an early partner of Meta's Muse. Meta said users can ask the agent to explore travel, ticketing and reservation options through the airline. "People treat agent risk as one-size-fits-all rather than matching the security needed to the actual task," said Yat Siu, executive chairman and co-founder of Animoca Brands. He said agents could help consumers act on their intentions and help businesses reach customers directly, but the risks vary by task. "There's a much higher risk around an agent able to move meaningful sums of money or access sensitive personal data, than one making your restaurant reservations," Siu said. "The reality is that, just like internet applications to date, agents require tiered safeguards."
